clinicalPearls: The commonest extragonadal site for germ cell tumours, arising in the anterior mediastinum, and predominantly affecting young men
Divided into seminomatous and non-seminomatous types, which differ markedly in treatment and outlook

Non-seminomatous tumours characteristically raise serum alpha-fetoprotein and/or beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin, whereas pure seminoma may show a modestly raised beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin but a normal alpha-fetoprotein
There is a recognised association with Klinefelter syndrome, so karyotype should be considered in young men
Testicular examination and imaging are needed to confirm a primary mediastinal origin rather than a metastasis from a testicular primary
Seminomas are highly chemosensitive and radiosensitive with a good prognosis, while non-seminomatous tumours require cisplatin-based chemotherapy often followed by resection of residual disease
A raised alpha-fetoprotein essentially excludes pure seminoma and mandates management as a non-seminomatous tumour
reference.pathophysiology: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumours are believed to originate from primordial germ cells that became arrested in the mediastinum during their embryonic migration along the midline. These pluripotent cells can give rise to the full spectrum of germ cell tumours, from mature teratoma through seminoma to malignant non-seminomatous types such as yolk sac tumour, embryonal carcinoma, and choriocarcinoma. Malignant elements secrete alpha-fetoprotein or beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin, which serve as diagnostic and monitoring markers. The association with Klinefelter syndrome implicates the extra X chromosome in the pathogenesis of mediastinal disease in affected young men.
additionalDifferentials: Metastasis from a testicular germ cell primary
additionalInvestigations: Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin, with lactate dehydrogenase
Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis for staging
Testicular examination and scrotal ultrasound to exclude a testicular primary
Biopsy with immunohistochemistry when markers are non-diagnostic
Karyotype to evaluate for Klinefelter syndrome in young men
redFlags: Superior vena caval obstruction or airway compromise from a bulky mass
Markedly elevated tumour markers indicating aggressive non-seminomatous disease
Rapid growth with distant metastases at presentation
Development of a somatic malignancy within a teratomatous component
reference.prognosis: Mediastinal seminoma has an excellent prognosis with chemotherapy and radiotherapy, whereas primary mediastinal non-seminomatous tumours carry a poorer outlook than their gonadal counterparts and require intensive chemotherapy with resection of residual masses.
pitfalls: Failing to measure tumour markers before treatment, losing baseline and diagnostic information
Treating a marker-positive tumour as a seminoma when a raised alpha-fetoprotein indicates non-seminomatous disease
Overlooking a testicular primary and mislabelling the tumour as extragonadal
Not considering Klinefelter syndrome in a young man with a mediastinal germ cell tumour
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy, such as bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin, as the systemic mainstay for both seminomatous and non-seminomatous tumours
Surgical resection of residual masses after chemotherapy for non-seminomatous tumours, given their poorer response
Serial alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin and lactate dehydrogenase to guide treatment and monitor response
Sperm banking and fertility counselling before gonadotoxic chemotherapy
Exclude a testicular primary and offer karyotyping for Klinefelter syndrome in young men
Manage superior vena cava obstruction and airway compromise from mass effect as acute complications
Coordinate care through a germ-cell and thoracic oncology multidisciplinary team
